en.explanation: A VXLAN Network Identifier (VNI) identifies the overlay L2/L3 segment in the fabric—not a local VLAN ID alone or a BGP ASN.

en.question: GETVPN (GDOI) is designed for:
options: The public Internet with NAT, which rewrites the source IP along the path
Private WAN (MPLS) with group IPsec while preserving original headers
Wi-Fi only, with no group IPsec overlay protecting the private WAN
IPv6 link-local traffic, confined to the segment and never routed
en.explanation: GETVPN uses a key server to distribute keys; original IP headers stay visible, which suits MPLS cores needing to route on real IPs.

en.question: QoS LLQ (Low Latency Queue) is typically for:
options: Bulk backups queued at low priority inside CBWFQ
Real-time voice/video (priority queue)
Best-effort HTTP in class-default, with no strict queue
Routing updates only, with no real-time voice or video
en.explanation: In a policy-map, priority enables LLQ (strict priority) for a class and is usually policed so voice cannot starve other queues.

en.question: WRED avoids:
options: BGP blackholing when a dropped neighbor session withdraws the prefix from the Loc-RIB
Global tail drop by dropping probabilistically by DSCP before the queue is full
RIP loops caused by counting to infinity on a distance-vector routing update
NTP failure that leaves router clocks unsynchronized across the routing domain
en.explanation: WRED drops packets early with per-class/weight thresholds to signal TCP congestion before the queue tail-drops everything.

en.question: In a Cisco SD-WAN fabric, what identifies a TLOC?
options: Only the vEdge system-IP, omitting the transport color and the encapsulation
The combination of system-IP, color, and encapsulation (e.g. ipsec/gre)
Only the site-ID set in vManage, without system-IP, color, or encapsulation
The MAC address of the transport interface, instead of system-IP, color, and encapsulation
en.explanation: A TLOC (Transport Locator) is identified by system-IP + color + encapsulation; that tuple is how the control/overlay refers to a transport.

en.question: In an iBGP network with route reflectors, what is the main effect of configuring a client under an RR?
options: The client no longer needs any eBGP sessions with external peers outside the AS
The RR can reflect iBGP routes among clients without an iBGP full mesh
The RR automatically disables route aggregation inside the local BGP process
Clients always prefer the eBGP routes learned from the RR over every other path
en.explanation: Route reflectors scale iBGP: the RR reflects routes learned from clients to other clients/nonclients, avoiding a full mesh.

en.question: How does LLQ differ from plain CBWFQ for real-time voice?
options: LLQ removes all policing from the network, disabling the implicit priority-class policer and the shape rates of every other CBWFQ class on the egress policy-map
LLQ adds a strict-priority queue so voice can dequeue ahead of CBWFQ classes (often with a policer to limit priority bandwidth)
Plain CBWFQ always prefers voice over LLQ, dequeuing class-default ahead of the strict-priority queue even while the egress link is congested
LLQ only works on Frame Relay, because the strict-priority queue requires FRTS maps and cannot be applied on Ethernet or other interface encapsulations
en.explanation: LLQ = CBWFQ plus a priority queue. Voice/video get low latency; a priority policer prevents the priority class from starving other queues.

en.question: In Cisco Catalyst Center (DNA Center) Assurance, client health scores primarily help you:
options: Replace OSPF with static routes automatically in the campus control plane, with no operator review of the paths
See onboarding, connectivity, and application experience issues for wired/wireless clients over time
Disable the NetFlow collectors that export traffic flows from access switches and wireless access points
Force every access point into Monitor Mode, taking those radios out of service for wireless clients
en.explanation: Assurance aggregates telemetry (onboarding, RSSI, DHCP/AAA, app experience) into client/device health so you can troubleshoot trends and failures, not rewrite routing.

en.question: Model-Driven Telemetry (MDT) with gRPC/dial-out is preferred over classic SNMP polling mainly because it:
options: Streams subscribed YANG-modeled data continuously (push) with lower overhead and richer structured updates than repeated SNMP GETs
It works only on Frame Relay interfaces, because gRPC dial-out requires DLCI and LMI to export YANG models instead of running over Ethernet or IP
It replaces BGP on the control plane with YANG notifications, stopping prefix advertisement and using only gRPC subscriptions as the routing protocol
It removes the need for any collector or subscription, publishing YANG telemetry as a local broadcast with no gRPC dial-out destination or subscribed model
en.explanation: MDT uses YANG models and subscriptions (often gRPC dial-out or dial-in) to push telemetry to collectors. Compared with SNMP polling, you get continuous, structured updates with less chatter and better scale for modern assurance.

en.question: IEEE 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) improves high-density WLAN efficiency primarily with:
options: Disabling DFS channels in every regulatory domain, removing dynamic 5 GHz spectrum so clients are served without airtime scheduling
Replacing CAPWAP with plain Layer-2 bridging only between the AP and the WLC, removing the centralized WLAN control and data tunnel
OFDMA, MU-MIMO enhancements, BSS coloring, and Target Wake Time to serve more clients with less airtime contention
Mandatory WEP encryption on every SSID, using shared RC4 keys, as the method that reduces airtime contention in a dense WLAN
en.explanation: 802.11ax focuses on efficiency in dense environments: OFDMA schedules multi-user resource units, improved MU-MIMO, BSS coloring reduces co-channel interference impact, and TWT saves client power. It is not about dropping CAPWAP or using WEP.

en.question: What is the main operational reason to use ERSPAN instead of local SPAN?
options: To encapsulate mirrored traffic in GRE and send it across an IP network to a remote analyzer
To encrypt the control plane with IPsec by default, protecting BPDUs and adjacencies instead of copies
To replace NetFlow sampling entirely, stopping flow export and using only the mirror session as traffic accounting
To disable STP on the monitored VLAN, stopping BPDUs in that VLAN before they are copied to the analyzer
en.explanation: ERSPAN (Encapsulated Remote SPAN) GRE-encapsulates mirrored frames so a central packet analyzer can receive copies from switches elsewhere in the IP fabric. Local SPAN stays on the same switch; RSPAN uses a VLAN.

en.question: In Cisco wireless FlexConnect, what does local switching achieve at a remote branch AP?
options: Forces every user frame back to the WLC over the CAPWAP data tunnel before that frame can exit onto the branch LAN
Disables every SSID on the AP as soon as the CAPWAP tunnel drops, even when local switching and local authentication are set
Bridges client data to the local wired VLAN at the AP when configured, even if the WLC path is constrained
Converts the remote AP into a full BGP route reflector that reflects the branch iBGP routes to each associated wireless client
en.explanation: FlexConnect (H-REAP) local switching lets the AP bridge client traffic onto a local branch VLAN, reducing WAN hairpinning to the controller. Central switching tunnels user data to the WLC; local auth/switching options cover WAN failure modes.

en.question: What does IPv6 RA Guard protect against on an access switch?
options: It blocks all IPv6 traffic on the access port forever, allowing only DHCPv6 and dropping data, ND, and SLAAC messages
It filters rogue Router Advertisements on access ports so only trusted ports may announce prefixes/gateways
It replaces SLAAC with mandatory static addressing on every host and also rejects legitimate Router Advertisements on trusted ports
It automatically encrypts Neighbor Discovery with IPsec on each access port, ciphering RS, RA, NS, and NA without filtering rogue ads
en.explanation: RA Guard (IPv6 First Hop Security) drops or blocks unexpected Router Advertisements on untrusted access ports, stopping rogue devices from advertising fake prefixes or default gateways. Trusted uplink/router ports are allowed to send RAs. It complements DHCPv6 Guard and ND inspection.

en.question: In Cisco SD-WAN, what is the primary role of the vBond orchestrator?
options: It alone forwards every user data packet across the underlay, instead of the WAN Edges sending that traffic to each other
It replaces every WAN edge router with a Layer-2 bridge, removing OMP, TLOCs, and the SD-WAN overlay between sites
It only stores NetFlow records exported by the WAN Edges for compliance, without authenticating devices or doing onboarding
It authenticates and introduces WAN Edge devices to the overlay (vSmart/vManage), enabling secure onboarding
en.explanation: vBond is the orchestrator: WAN Edges authenticate to it first; vBond then tells them how to reach vSmart (control) and vManage (management). Data plane traffic stays between edges (often with IPsec); vSmart distributes control policy via OMP. vBond is critical for zero-touch bring-up and NAT traversal assistance.

en.question: In Cisco ACI, what is an Endpoint Group (EPG)?
options: A group of endpoints (VMs, bare metal, containers, etc.) that share the same policy treatment—typically mapped to a VLAN/VXLAN segment inside a Bridge Domain
The physical spine switch that replaces the APIC controller cluster, taking over fabric management alone and programming policy for every tenant and application
A BGP community that ACI copies unchanged into every WAN edge, tagging L3Out routes instead of grouping endpoints that should receive the same policy treatment
A NetFlow sampler template stored only on the border leaf, used to export L3Out flows rather than gathering VMs, bare metal, or containers under the same policy
en.explanation: An EPG is the fundamental policy object for endpoints that should be treated alike. Endpoints in an EPG live under a Bridge Domain (and VRF/tenant hierarchy). Communication between EPGs is controlled by contracts (provided/consumed), not by simply sharing a BD. The APIC still remains the controller; spines are fabric underlay, not EPGs.

en.question: In Cisco ACI, how do two EPGs normally communicate in a secure, policy-driven way?
options: They always flood all traffic in the underlay, with no filters or contracts, as soon as the two EPGs share only the same tenant name
Only if both EPGs are configured as OSPF neighbors on the same loopback, exchanging network LSAs instead of using contracts and filters
Through contracts: one EPG provides a contract and the other consumes it, allowing specific traffic (filters) between them
By enabling classic PVST+ Root Guard on every leaf downlink so the STP election opens traffic between the EPGs without any contract
en.explanation: ACI uses a whitelist model between EPGs: contracts define which traffic is allowed (filters/subjects). A provider EPG offers a contract; a consumer EPG consumes it. Sharing a Bridge Domain alone does not open arbitrary East-West access. This is application-centric policy, not classic VLAN ACLs alone or STP features.

en.question: In Cisco ACI, what is a Bridge Domain (BD) primarily responsible for?
options: Acting as the L2 forwarding construct (broadcast/unknown unicast/multicast scope) that EPGs attach to, often with a subnet/SVI gateway
Terminating every BGP session with external SPINE peers only, treating the Bridge Domain as a transit AS that advertises routes outside the ACI fabric
Replacing the APIC controller cluster with a single leaf switch that becomes the only management point for the fabric, the tenant, and the EPGs
Encrypting the tenant contracts with WPA3-Personal, applying SAE on each Bridge Domain to protect East-West traffic between attached EPGs
en.explanation: A Bridge Domain is the ACI Layer-2 construct: flooding scope, often holding the gateway subnet for connected EPGs. EPGs classify endpoints; contracts control EPG-to-EPG policy; VRFs separate L3 contexts. The BD is not the APIC, not BGP-only spine peering, and not a wireless cipher.

en.question: What is Guest Shell on Cisco IOS XE used for?
options: A replacement for the hardware TCAM on every Catalyst switch, so packet forwarding depends only on Python scripts inside the container
A wireless SSID defined in IOS XE that permanently disables 802.1X and leaves the WLAN open, with no Linux container and no Python
A CentOS/Linux container environment on-box to run Python scripts, yum packages, and network automation tools alongside IOS XE
A BGP community configured in IOS XE that always sets Local Preference to 0 on learned routes, without running Python scripts or yum packages
en.explanation: Guest Shell is an on-box Linux container (often CentOS-based) on IOS XE where you can run Python, install packages, and use guestshell/run commands for automation without leaving the device. It complements EEM/on-box Python but does not replace TCAM, redefine SSIDs, or set BGP communities by itself.

en.question: What is Cisco pyATS primarily used for in network automation and operations?
options: As a Python test and validation framework (often with Genie) to parse device state, run checks, and regress network changes safely
Replacing the underlay IGP with a proprietary Python-only routing protocol on every PE, dropping OSPF, IS-IS, and BGP on each fabric edge router before convergence
As the only supported GUI to configure ACI contracts, EPGs, filters, and tenants inside APIC, pushing fabric policy instead of running tests
As a replacement for RADIUS when doing 802.1X on wireless, validating client EAP, the supplicant certificate, and the VLAN assigned to the SSID
en.explanation: pyATS (often paired with Genie parsers/models) is Cisco’s Python framework for automated network testing: connect to devices, snapshot/parse operational state, diff before/after, and build reusable test suites for CI/CD or change windows. It is not a routing protocol, not the ACI contract GUI, and not an 802.1X/RADIUS replacement.

en.question: In Cisco ISE, what does a posture assessment typically check before (or as part of) granting full network access?
options: Only whether the switchport is in err-disable because of BPDU Guard, treating that port state as the sole posture criterion before granting the endpoint its full access VLAN, ignoring antivirus and the OS patch level
Only the OSPF area ID configured on the user’s laptop, as if posture compliance depended on the endpoint routing process rather than antivirus, patches, or disk encryption
Whether the endpoint meets security policy (for example antivirus status, OS patch level, disk encryption, or a required agent) so non-compliant devices can be quarantined or remediated
Whether the SSID name is hidden, which alone proves the client is trusted, skipping antivirus, OS patch level, disk encryption, a host firewall, and any required posture agent
en.explanation: ISE posture evaluates the health/compliance of the connecting endpoint (via AnyConnect/secure client posture module or similar) against policy—AV, patches, firewall, encryption, etc. Non-compliant hosts can get a restricted VLAN/ACL and remediation portal. It is unrelated to BPDU Guard err-disable, OSPF area IDs on laptops, or hiding the SSID.

en.question: In Cisco SD-Access, what is the primary role of the Control Plane Node?
options: It terminates all user DHCP and NAT for every edge switch in hardware only, without hosting the LISP Map-Server or resolving any EID-to-RLOC mappings in the fabric overlay
It hosts the LISP Map-Server/Map-Resolver function: edge nodes register endpoint EID-to-RLOC mappings and query the control plane to locate destinations in the fabric
It replaces Spanning Tree by flooding every unknown MAC to the entire underlay, instead of edge nodes querying the LISP control plane to locate destinations
It is only a management GUI and never participates in the data or control plane, leaving all EID-to-RLOC registration and resolution to Catalyst Center
en.explanation: SD-Access uses LISP for the fabric control plane. Control Plane Nodes act as Map-Server/Map-Resolver: fabric edge nodes register EIDs (endpoints) to RLOCs (edge/border locators) and resolve remote EIDs before VXLAN encapsulation. They are not DHCP/NAT appliances, do not flood unknown MACs like classic Ethernet learning floods, and are not merely a GUI (Catalyst Center/DNA Center is the orchestrator).

en.question: In a Cisco IOS zone-based policy firewall (ZBFW), how is traffic between interfaces controlled?
options: Every interface must be placed in VLAN 1, and ACLs on the VTY lines filter transit traffic, with no security zones assigned and no zone-pair policy-maps to inspect flows, as if the zone firewall did not exist on the router
ZBFW only inspects multicast PIM joins and ignores unicast TCP/UDP, so sessions between the inside zone and the outside zone are neither classified, permitted, nor inspected by any inspect policy
You configure classic ip inspect CBAC globally; zones are ignored when NAT is enabled, and no zone-pair with a class-map controls traffic between the interfaces of the source and destination zones

Interfaces are assigned to security zones; a zone-pair with a policy-map (class-maps) defines what is inspected/allowed between a source zone and a destination zone (intra-zone traffic is typically allowed by default)
en.explanation: ZBFW groups interfaces into zones. Inter-zone traffic requires an explicit zone-pair and a policy (class-map/policy-map) that permits/inspects flows from source zone to destination zone. Same-zone traffic is usually allowed without a zone-pair. It is not limited to PIM, does not rely on VTY ACLs for transit forwarding, and is distinct from legacy interface CBAC-only designs.

en.question: In a Cisco ISE / RADIUS deployment, what is Change of Authorization (CoA) used for?
options: To permanently replace TACACS+ with RADIUS for all device CLI logins, using CoA as the only method of administrator authentication and command authorization on every managed network device
To download the switch IOS image over TFTP after every successful 802.1X session, treating CoA as the NAD software-upgrade path rather than dynamic authorization
To let the policy server push an update to an already-authenticated session (for example reauthenticate, terminate, or change VLAN/ACL/SGT) without waiting for the next client login
To elect the STP root bridge based on the RADIUS shared secret, making CoA the bridge-priority and path-cost criterion across the Layer-2 domain of the access switch
en.explanation: CoA (RFC 5176 dynamic authorization) lets ISE/RADIUS send unsolicited messages to the NAD so an active session can be reauthenticated, disconnected, or given a new authorization result (VLAN, dACL, SGT, etc.). It is not a TACACS replacement policy, not an IOS image download mechanism, and unrelated to STP root election.

en.question: What problem does Cisco OTV (Overlay Transport Virtualization) primarily solve?
options: Extending Layer-2 VLANs / Ethernet segments across a Layer-3 data-center interconnect while containing STP and reducing flooding compared with a naive long L2 stretch
Replacing BGP with a proprietary Cisco-only underlay IGP in the Internet core, rather than extending Layer-2 VLANs across a Layer-3 data-center interconnect
Providing Power over Ethernet to servers in a leaf-spine fabric, powering hosts instead of extending Ethernet segments and containing STP across the DCI between sites
Encrypting DNS queries between recursive resolvers and authoritative servers, without extending VLANs or containing STP domains over the interconnect
en.explanation: OTV is a MAC-routing overlay used to extend VLANs between data centers over an IP transport, with mechanisms that help contain STP domains and control ARP/unknown unicast flooding versus a simple stretched L2 link. It is not an Internet underlay IGP, not PoE, and not DNS encryption.

en.question: In BGP, what does Graceful Restart (often paired with NSF on Cisco platforms) primarily allow during a control-plane restart?
options: Automatically converting all eBGP sessions into iBGP so the AS number can be removed, instead of preserving the FIB and stale routes during the control-plane restart
Preserving forwarding (FIB) and asking peers to keep routes marked stale until the restarting speaker recovers and refreshes the RIB, reducing traffic loss
Forcing every peer to clear its entire BGP table and reconverge from scratch for consistency, dropping stale routes and the forwarding already installed in the FIB
Replacing TCP session keepalive with BFD-only detection and deleting all MPLS labels, rather than keeping forwarding while the restarting speaker refreshes the RIB
en.explanation: BGP Graceful Restart / NSF keeps the data plane forwarding while the control plane restarts. Peers retain stale routes for a restart timer; after recovery, End-of-RIB and updates refresh state. It does not convert eBGP to iBGP, and it aims to avoid a full destructive reconvergence storm rather than force one.

en.question: In a Cisco Secure Firewall (formerly Firepower) deployment, what is the primary role of FMC (Firewall Management Center)?
options: Acting as the default gateway and NAT boundary for every access VLAN in the campus, forwarding user traffic instead of deploying access policy to the Firepower sensors
Terminating all site-to-site IPsec tunnels so threat sensors never see encrypted traffic, acting as the mandatory VPN hub for every remote peer
Replacing ISE for 802.1X authentication of switch access ports, issuing VLAN, dACL, and SGT results in place of the identity policy server
Centralized policy, event, and device management for managed Secure Firewall / threat defense sensors (push policies, collect events, coordinate updates)
en.explanation: FMC is the manager: it authors and deploys access control / intrusion / malware policies, inventories devices, and aggregates events/health. The sensors (FTD/Secure Firewall) sit in the data path. FMC is not the campus default gateway, not a mandatory IPsec hub for every tunnel, and not a replacement for ISE 802.1X on switch ports.

en.question: In a VXLAN fabric, what do a VTEP and a VNI represent?
options: The VTEP is the VXLAN tunnel endpoint that encapsulates/decapsulates frames; the VNI (VXLAN Network Identifier) is the 24-bit segment ID that separates overlay Layer 2 networks
The VTEP is only a multicast group address, and the VNI is the underlay OSPF process ID, with no Ethernet encapsulation and no separation of overlay segments in a VXLAN EVPN fabric
The VNI is the physical switch serial number, and the VTEP is a RADIUS shared secret, with no role as a VXLAN tunnel endpoint or segment identifier
Both terms mean the same thing: the outer UDP destination port 4789, without distinguishing the encapsulating endpoint from the 24-bit overlay ID
en.explanation: A VTEP (VXLAN Tunnel Endpoint) sits at the edge of the overlay—often on a leaf or hypervisor—and performs VXLAN encapsulation/decapsulation. The VNI is a 24-bit identifier that distinguishes overlay segments (analogous in role to a VLAN ID, but with a much larger space). Multicast/underlay routing may help BUM replication, but that is not what “VTEP” or “VNI” mean; neither is a serial number, RADIUS secret, or merely UDP/4789.

en.question: In Cisco SD-WAN (Viptela architecture), which trio of roles best matches vManage, vSmart, and vBond?
options: vManage = data-plane forwarding ASIC on every WAN Edge; vSmart = underlay DHCP server for the IPsec tunnels; vBond = campus wireless controller for the APs, with no management UI, no OMP overlay policy, and no WAN Edge onboarding

vManage = underlay IGP only (OSPF or BGP) between transports; vSmart = per-site egress NAT gateway; vBond = syslog collector for edges and controllers, with no central orchestration, no OMP overlay routing, and no initial authentication

vManage = centralized management/orchestration UI and device config; vSmart = control-plane policy and overlay routing intelligence; vBond = initial authentication/orchestration facilitator that helps bring devices into the overlay

All three appliances forward user packets in the data plane at each site and never participate in control or management, leaving centralized policy, device templates, and secure onboarding to the WAN Edge routers
en.explanation: In the classic Cisco SD-WAN controller split: vManage is the management/orchestration system (GUI, templates, monitoring); vSmart handles control-plane overlay intelligence and centralized policy; vBond assists securely onboarding/authenticating WAN Edge devices and pointing them to the rest of the fabric. Edge routers (vEdge/cEdge) carry the data plane—not the three controllers as packet forwarders.

en.question: In Cisco IOS/IOS XE, what is a route map most commonly used for?
options: Matching routes or traffic with conditions (prefix lists, ACLs, metrics, tags, etc.) and then applying set actions—for example in redistribution, PBR, or BGP attribute manipulation
Replacing the FIB entirely with a static list of MAC addresses learned from CDP neighbors, which the data plane uses to forward frames instead of the CEF table
Terminating SSL/TLS sessions on the route processor so that every packet is decrypted in software on the RP itself, before any CEF lookup or before programming the egress adjacency
Electing the OSPF Designated Router on broadcast segments when hello timers differ, by choosing the neighbor whose dead interval advertised in the hello packet is the largest
en.explanation: A route map is a sequenced list of match/set clauses. It is widely used to control redistribution (which prefixes, with what metric/tag), policy-based routing, and BGP path-attribute changes. It is not a MAC/FIB substitute, not an SSL offload feature on the RP, and not the OSPF DR election mechanism.

en.question: What is the main purpose of BGP route dampening?
options: To temporarily suppress flapping prefixes and cut repeated withdrawal churn
To convert every eBGP session into iBGP so each edge router can share a full Internet table without using confederations or route reflectors
To replace TCP session keepalives with BFD-only failure detection on every BGP neighbor under all address families
To force MED and local preference to identical values so exit traffic always prefers the peer with the lowest router ID
en.explanation: BGP route dampening assigns a penalty when a prefix flaps; if the penalty exceeds a suppress threshold the route is withheld until the penalty decays below a reuse threshold. That limits control-plane churn from unstable peers or links. It does not turn eBGP into iBGP, replace keepalives with BFD-only, or equalize MED/local-pref.

en.question: In Zero Trust designs, what does ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access) primarily provide for application access?
options: A full Internet BGP table on every laptop so remote users never need a corporate VPN or any identity check at all
Unconditional trust for any device that once passed NAC on campus, with no further session re-evaluation afterward
Layer-2 flooding of all application traffic across every campus VLAN so east-west flows stay completely unfiltered
Identity-aware, per-app access brokered after continuous authz—without exposing the whole internal network
en.explanation: ZTNA brokers access to specific applications based on user/device identity and policy, typically without placing the user on the full internal network like a classic VPN. It aligns with continuous authentication/authorization. It is not shipping a full BGP table to laptops, not one-time NAC forever-trust, and not L2 flooding of app traffic.

en.question: How does passwordless authentication (e.g., FIDO2/WebAuthn or platform passkeys) mainly differ from classic MFA that pairs a password with an OTP?
options: Passwordless proves a crypto authenticator (often phishing-resistant) without a reusable password; classic MFA still centers on password plus a second factor
Passwordless permanently deletes every Active Directory user object so the campus can only use shared local administrator accounts on every workstation forever after rollout
Passwordless only works when users authenticate over serial console cables to the router, while OTP-based MFA only works after OSPF has fully converged on all PE routers in the VRF
Classic MFA always negotiates quantum-safe lattice keys on every TLS handshake, while passwordless only stores cleartext user passwords inside public DNS TXT records for the realm
en.explanation: Passwordless/FIDO2-style auth uses public-key cryptography bound to an authenticator or platform, so users are not transmitting a reusable password. Classic MFA still typically starts with a password and adds OTP/push/SMS. It is not about deleting AD, serial consoles vs OSPF, or storing passwords in DNS.

en.question: What is the main purpose of VRF route leaking between two VRFs on the same PE/router?
options: To erase every MPLS label in the global table so the PE can only forward frames with IEEE 802.1Q tags from the access layer
To force all VRFs to share a single OSPF process ID that must equal the BGP AS number or else iBGP sessions refuse to establish
To convert every VRF into a VLAN on the same switch stack so east-west traffic never needs an IP address again
To selectively share specific prefixes (e.g., shared services) across VRF routing tables without merging the whole tables
en.explanation: VRF route leaking (import/export of selected routes, often via route-targets or static) lets shared services—DNS, DHCP, management—reach multiple VRFs while keeping the rest of each VRF isolated. It is not about erasing MPLS labels, tying OSPF process IDs to the BGP AS, or turning VRFs into VLANs.

en.question: In MPLS Layer-3 VPNs, what is the main role of a route target (RT) extended community?
options: It controls which VPN routes a PE imports into or exports from a VRF, enabling selective sharing across VPNs
It permanently deletes the global routing table so the PE can forward only unlabeled IPv4 frames from the access layer
It replaces LDP with STP so every PE elects a single root bridge before any VPN label can be advertised at all
It encrypts customer payloads with a key equal to the BGP AS number so CE routers never need IPsec tunnels
en.explanation: Route targets are BGP extended communities that tag VPN routes for export and match them on import into VRFs, defining which sites share routes. They do not wipe the global table, replace LDP with STP, or derive payload encryption from the AS number.

en.question: What problem does Segment Routing (SR) mainly aim to simplify compared with classic MPLS that relies on LDP (or RSVP-TE) for label distribution?
options: It permanently removes the IP underlay so every packet must be bridged at Layer 2 across the whole SP backbone
It replaces BGP entirely with a proprietary IGP that cannot carry VPN routes or internet prefixes anymore
It forces every PE to run a full mesh of GRE tunnels before any label can be imposed on customer prefixes
It encodes the path as segments (often advertised in the IGP), reducing need for LDP/RSVP-TE state per LSP
en.explanation: Segment Routing steers traffic using an ordered list of segments (node/adjacency/prefix SIDs), typically distributed via the IGP (or BGP), so operators can do TE-like steering with less per-LSP signaling state than classic LDP or RSVP-TE. It does not remove the IP underlay, replace BGP, or require a GRE mesh before labels work.

en.question: In BGP, what problem does Outbound Route Filtering (ORF) mainly help reduce?
options: It lets a receiver push prefix filters to the sender so unwanted UPDATE churn is cut before those routes are advertised inbound
It replaces TCP MD5 and GTSM on every eBGP session so ORF alone authenticates peers without any shared secret or TTL check configured
It converts all iBGP full-mesh peers into route-reflector clients automatically when the ORF capability is negotiated on the session once
It forces every BGP speaker to advertise only default routes and withdraws all more-specific prefixes from the global table immediately
en.explanation: ORF (often prefix-list based) lets the receiving BGP speaker advertise its inbound filter to the sender, so the sender suppresses UPDATEs the receiver would discard anyway—saving bandwidth and CPU. ORF does not replace session security (MD5/GTSM), does not auto-convert a full mesh into route reflectors, and does not force default-only advertisements globally.

en.question: In BGP, what problem does the Additional Paths (add-path) capability mainly help solve?
options: It replaces every eBGP multihop session with pure iBGP so AS-path length is ignored forever during best-path selection on all speakers in the AS
It forces each PE to originate a default route into every VRF automatically, removing any need for route-target import/export in MPLS Layer-3 VPNs
It converts MED into a fully transitive attribute so every downstream AS must prefer exactly the same exit point that the local AS already selected before
It lets a BGP speaker advertise more than one path for the same prefix to a peer, improving path diversity and failover when the primary path is lost
en.explanation: Classic BGP advertises only the best path per prefix to a neighbor. Add-path allows advertising additional paths for the same NLRI so peers can keep backups ready—improving diversity and convergence. It does not replace eBGP multihop, force VRF defaults instead of RTs, or make MED transitive.

en.question: What is the main goal of MPLS Traffic Engineering (MPLS-TE) compared with plain IP/IGP shortest-path forwarding?
options: Steer selected traffic onto constrained LSPs (often RSVP-TE) that can follow bandwidth or affinity rules, not only the IGP shortest path
Replace every IGP adjacency with a permanent GRE tunnel so that OSPF and IS-IS no longer need to exchange LSAs or hellos on the underlay across the entire provider core
Force all customer VRF routes to use a single global BGP next-hop that ignores TE tunnels, affinities, administrative weights, and any reserved bandwidth on the core
Encrypt every labeled packet with MACsec on the PE-CE edge only, which vendors treat as mandatory before any TE tunnel can be signaled or admitted across the MPLS core
en.explanation: MPLS-TE builds constrained LSPs (commonly via RSVP-TE) so traffic can take engineered paths meeting bandwidth/affinity constraints rather than pure IGP SPF. It does not replace IGPs with GRE-only, ignore TE for a single BGP next-hop, or require MACsec before TE signaling.

en.question: What does BGP Prefix Independent Convergence (PIC) edge mainly aim to improve?
options: It permanently deletes every iBGP session so the edge router can only learn prefixes from an IGP default route and never retain any BGP multipath entries in the CEF forwarding table
It forces MED and local preference to identical values on all peers so traffic-engineering communities can never influence exit selection again on any production edge router
It precomputes a backup path in the FIB/CEF so that, after a PE-CE or peering failure, forwarding can switch to the alternate next hop with less per-prefix recalculation delay
It replaces BGP entirely with OSPF Type-5 LSAs flooded from the Internet edge so external prefixes converge only through a full SPF run on every local ABR in the area
en.explanation: BGP PIC edge keeps a precomputed backup path so failover after an edge/peering failure needs far less per-prefix work—faster convergence in the FIB. It does not delete iBGP, freeze MED/local-pref, or replace BGP with OSPF external LSAs.

en.question: Two routers perform mutual redistribution between OSPF and EIGRP. What is a common way to stop routes from looping back into the domain they came from?
options: Raise the OSPF reference bandwidth on both routers so that redistributed routes always have a higher cost than native routes and are never installed again
Tag routes as they are redistributed (e.g., set tag 110) and use route-maps on the other redistribution point to deny routes carrying that tag
Enable BFD between the two redistribution routers so that any looping route is detected as a failed neighbor and is removed within a few milliseconds
Configure the OSPF area as totally stubby so that external LSAs are blocked and EIGRP never learns any route that originated inside the OSPF domain
en.explanation: Route tags mark where a prefix was redistributed; a route-map at the other boundary matches the tag and denies it, preventing feedback loops and suboptimal paths. Reference bandwidth and BFD do not track route origin, and a totally stubby area blocks LSAs into that area, not redistribution feedback at an ASBR.

en.question: Given ip prefix-list LAB permit 10.0.0.0/8 ge 24 le 24, which of these routes is permitted?
options: 10.0.0.0/8, because the base prefix and its length always match exactly whenever the ge and le keywords are set in the same entry
10.1.0.0/16, because any prefix inside 10.0.0.0/8 that is shorter than /24 is matched before the ge 24 condition is evaluated
10.1.2.128/25, because the ge 24 keyword matches any prefix length of /24 or longer, regardless of the le 24 upper limit set
10.1.2.0/24, because the first 8 bits match 10.0.0.0/8 and the prefix length is exactly /24, which is both ge 24 and le 24
en.explanation: With ge and le, the network bits must match the base (first 8 bits = 10) and the prefix length must fall in the range given; ge 24 le 24 means exactly /24. So only 10.1.2.0/24 matches. /8 and /16 are too short, and /25 is longer than le 24 allows.

en.question: Two customer sites both use BGP AS 65010 and connect to a provider's MPLS L3VPN (AS 64500). Routes from site 1 never appear at site 2. Which provider-side fix is commonly used?
options: Configure next-hop-self on the PE routers, because the CE drops any route whose next hop is not directly connected to it
Configure neighbor as-override on the PE toward each CE, so the PE replaces AS 65010 in the AS path with its own AS 64500
Configure remove-private-as on the CE routers, so AS 65010 is stripped before the routes are sent towards the provider PEs
Configure a route reflector on the PE routers, because iBGP split horizon is blocking the routes between the two sites
en.explanation: eBGP loop prevention makes the site 2 CE reject routes that already carry its own AS 65010. With as-override, the PE swaps the customer AS for the provider AS, so the CE accepts the route. The customer-side alternative is allowas-in on the CE. Next-hop-self, a route reflector or remove-private-as on the CE do not fix this AS-path check (remove-private-as on a CE would also leave its own AS in the path).

en.question: A BGP speaker advertises aggregate-address 10.0.0.0/8 as-set summary-only. What does the as-set keyword change in the aggregate that peers receive?
options: It builds an AS_SET in the AS_PATH from the more-specifics, so loop detection still sees those origin ASes
It forces every more-specific route to remain advertised with the aggregate toward all eBGP and iBGP peers
It sets the atomic-aggregate attribute and strips communities, so peers cannot tell which ASes originated the parts
It rewrites the next-hop of the aggregate to the local router-id and disables next-hop-self on all iBGP sessions
en.explanation: With as-set, the aggregate's AS_PATH includes an AS_SET unordered list of ASes from the suppressed more-specifics, preserving loop detection. summary-only suppresses advertising those more-specifics (so as-set does not keep them advertised). atomic-aggregate is separate; as-set does not itself strip communities or change next-hop/iBGP next-hop-self behavior.

en.question: In an MPLS L3VPN, a multihomed CE site is assigned a Site of Origin (SoO) value on the PE-CE VRF. What is the main purpose of SoO?
options: It replaces the route distinguisher so two VRFs can share one overlapping IPv4 prefix without needing a unique RD value in each VRF instance
It forces every PE to prefer eBGP PE-CE paths over iBGP VPNv4 paths by raising local preference to 200 for that SoO tag
It encrypts the VPNv4 update between PEs with a per-site IPsec SA derived from the SoO extended community value
It marks that site’s prefixes so a PE can block advertising those same routes back into the site and avoid loops
en.explanation: SoO is an extended community that marks routes as belonging to a particular customer site. On a multihomed site, PEs use it to recognize prefixes that originated at that site and avoid re-injecting them back toward the same site (routing loops / suboptimal re-entry). RD uniqueness is separate from SoO; SoO is not a local-preference knob and does not provide IPsec for VPNv4.

en.question: In an MPLS L3VPN, when is an OSPF sham-link between PE routers typically required?
options: When a backdoor OSPF link between two CE sites would otherwise be preferred over the intra-area path across the MPLS VPN backbone
When every CE must run BGP instead of OSPF so the PE can translate OSPF LSAs into VPNv4 routes with a unique RD per customer site
When LDP is disabled in the core and the only label distribution protocol left between P routers is RSVP-TE for unicast IPv4 traffic
When the customer VRF uses EIGRP as the PE-CE protocol and needs an OSPF adjacency only to carry multicast RPF check state
en.explanation: A sham-link creates an intra-area OSPF adjacency between PEs across the MPLS VPN so the backbone path looks intra-area. Without it, a real backdoor CE–CE OSPF link (also intra-area) can be preferred over the inter-area-looking VPN path. Sham-links are an OSPF PE-CE design tool, not a substitute for BGP-only PE-CE, LDP replacement, or EIGRP multicast RPF.

en.question: In a service-provider or large enterprise edge, what is Remotely Triggered Black Hole (RTBH) filtering mainly used for?
options: It mirrors a copy of every customer packet into a local SPAN session so NetFlow records can be rebuilt offline after flaps
It forces all iBGP speakers to become route-reflector clients of each other so the classic full-mesh requirement disappears
It replaces OSPF with IS-IS in the core by injecting a default route tagged only with the well-known community no-advertise
It quickly discards traffic to (or from) an attacked prefix by injecting a more-specific route that points to Null0
en.explanation: RTBH uses BGP (or similar) to inject a trigger route so edge routers black-hole an attacked destination (destination-based) or source (source-based with uRPF) via Null0. It is a fast DDoS mitigation technique, not SPAN/NetFlow rebuild, not a route-reflector substitute, and not an OSPF-to-IS-IS migration tool.

en.question: In a service-provider metro Ethernet design, what does VPLS (Virtual Private LAN Service) mainly provide to customers?
options: A multipoint Layer-2 Emulated LAN over an MPLS (or similar) core so distant sites appear to share one bridged Ethernet segment
A one-to-one IPsec tunnel per CE that replaces every customer VLAN with a unique VRF-lite table on each PE without any pseudowires at all
An OSPF Area 0 only inside the provider core that automatically redistributes every customer BGP prefix into IS-IS Level-1 everywhere
A unicast-only L3VPN that forbids broadcast and unknown-unicast flooding so Ethernet ARP can never cross the provider backbone links
en.explanation: VPLS emulates a shared LAN (multipoint L2 VPN) across a packet/MPLS backbone using pseudowires/VSI bridging so customer Ethernet domains can span sites. It is not per-CE IPsec replacing VRFs, not an OSPF Area 0 redistribution trick into IS-IS, and not a unicast-only L3VPN that bans ARP flooding.

en.question: In a VXLAN EVPN fabric, how do EVPN Route Type-2 and Route Type-5 mainly differ?
options: Type-2 only advertises multicast underlay PIM joins toward RPs, while Type-5 only carries Spanning Tree BPDUs between VTEPs across the fabric core links
Type-2 advertises MAC/IP host reachability for bridged endpoints, while Type-5 advertises IP prefixes for inter-subnet / L3VPN-style reachability
Type-2 replaces BGP entirely with IS-IS Level-1 flooding of entire MAC tables, while Type-5 is reserved for LDP label binding of every VLAN identifier
Type-2 and Type-5 are identical NLRI formats end-to-end; the only difference is whether the VTEP uses OSPF or EIGRP as the underlay IGP protocol
en.explanation: EVPN Type-2 (MAC/IP Advertisement) carries host MAC and optional IP bindings for L2/L2+L3 adjacency inside a VNI. Type-5 (IP Prefix Route) advertises prefixes for routing between subnets or external networks. They are not PIM-only vs BPDU carriers, not IS-IS/LDP substitutes, and not identical NLRI.

en.question: In an iBGP route-reflector design, what do the ORIGINATOR_ID and CLUSTER_LIST attributes mainly help prevent?
options: Routing loops and reflection of the same path back toward its originator inside the reflector cluster topology
All eBGP sessions from accepting MED values unless every peer also negotiates the add-path capability first
OSPF areas from forming virtual links whenever an RR client also runs IS-IS Level-2 on the same loopback address
IPv6 ND from installing neighbor entries unless the RR stamps every prefix with a unique Site-Local Scope identifier
en.explanation: ORIGINATOR_ID records the router that originated the route into the RR cluster; CLUSTER_LIST tracks clusters that reflected it. Together they let routers detect and drop looping reflections. They are not about eBGP MED/add-path gates, OSPF/IS-IS virtual links, or IPv6 ND Site-Local rules.

en.question: After changing an inbound BGP route-map, why is route refresh usually preferred over neighbor soft-reconfiguration inbound?
options: Route refresh asks the peer to resend routes without storing a full extra Adj-RIB-In copy, while soft-reconfiguration inbound keeps that duplicate
Route refresh only works for eBGP and always tears down TCP first, while soft-reconfiguration inbound is required before any iBGP session can come up at all
Soft-reconfiguration inbound never applies a new inbound policy at all, so only a hard clear can install updated route-map results into the Loc-RIB forever
Route refresh disables best-path selection until the peer finishes sending, while soft-reconfiguration inbound freezes the RIB-Out so no UPDATEs leave
en.explanation: Soft-reconfiguration inbound stores an extra unmodified Adj-RIB-In copy (memory cost). Route refresh (RFC 2918) asks the peer to resend so new inbound policy can be applied without that copy or a session reset. Soft-reconfig does apply policy on the stored copy; it is not eBGP-only magic.

en.question: Users behind a GRE over IPsec tunnel can open small web pages, but large downloads stall. Why is ip tcp adjust-mss (for example 1360) applied on the tunnel interface?
options: It raises the tunnel MTU above 1500 bytes so encapsulated packets can carry full Ethernet payloads without the physical link ever fragmenting them
It disables IPsec anti-replay checking for TCP flows, because large segments arrive out of order and would otherwise be dropped by the receiving peer
It rewrites the MSS in TCP SYN packets so endpoints send segments small enough to fit after tunnel overhead, avoiding fragmentation and PMTUD failures
It tells the router to clear the DF bit on every packet entering the tunnel, so oversized TCP segments are always fragmented by the router after encryption instead
en.explanation: Tunnel headers reduce usable MTU. ip tcp adjust-mss rewrites the MSS option in TCP SYNs passing through, so hosts send smaller segments that fit, avoiding fragmentation and broken PMTUD when ICMP is blocked. It does not raise MTU, disable anti-replay, or clear DF.

en.question: You want a router to automatically run show commands and save them whenever a specific interface logs a down event, with no external server. Which IOS feature fits best?
options: Configure SNMP read-only community strings, because read-only SNMP can execute CLI show commands locally and write their output to flash each time an interface changes state
Enable NetFlow on the interface, since NetFlow records are designed to run arbitrary EXEC commands and archive their text output automatically when a link transitions to down
Schedule a reload every few minutes, because reloading is the supported mechanism to capture interface state and the startup process writes diagnostics to flash on each boot
An Embedded Event Manager (EEM) applet triggered on the syslog pattern for that interface going down, running the show commands and saving the output locally
en.explanation: EEM applets watch events such as syslog patterns and run CLI actions on the device itself, so a link-down message can trigger show commands saved to flash with no external system. SNMP, NetFlow, and periodic reloads do not do local event-driven automation.

en.question: You need a BGP edge router to advertise a backup prefix to a peer only while a primary prefix is missing from the local BGP table. Which Cisco mechanism fits?
options: BGP conditional advertisement with an advertise-map tied to a non-exist-map (or exist-map), so the backup prefix is announced only when the watched primary prefix is absent (or present)
A static null0 route for the backup prefix with administrative distance 1, because a null route alone causes BGP to withdraw and re-advertise prefixes whenever the primary path flaps
Enabling BGP soft-reconfiguration inbound on every neighbour, because soft-reconfiguration stores a second RIB that automatically toggles outbound advertisements when prefixes disappear
Configuring maximum-prefix on the peer with a restart threshold, because hitting the prefix limit is the supported way to publish a backup route only during primary outages
en.explanation: Conditional advertisement uses advertise-map with non-exist-map or exist-map so a prefix is advertised only when another watched prefix is missing or present. Null0 routes, soft-reconfiguration, and maximum-prefix do not implement that conditional outbound logic.

en.question: On a point-to-point serial or Ethernet link you configure ip unnumbered Loopback0 under both ends. What is the main operational effect, and which constraint still applies?
options: Each end borrows a unique /32 from a DHCP pool so the link becomes a numbered /30 automatically, and OSPF refuses to advertise that borrowed address until a secondary IP is also assigned on the same interface for adjacency

ip unnumbered disables CEF on that interface and forces process switching for every packet, which is required before MPLS labels can be imposed on point-to-point WAN circuits in any production backbone design today

Both ends share one IPv4 address space borrowed from another interface, eliminating the need for a dedicated transit subnet, but you cannot ping the remote end by a distinct link IP because none exists on the wire at all in that design

Both ends borrow the IPv4 address of a referenced interface (often a loopback), so the link needs no dedicated transit subnet; routing still works for transit, yet you must not expect a unique on-link host address for each peer
en.explanation: ip unnumbered borrows the address of another interface so the point-to-point link needs no dedicated subnet; forwarding and IGPs can still use the link, but there is no unique on-wire host IP per peer. It does not invent DHCP /30s, does not require disabling CEF, and the precise wording is about borrowing rather than sharing one ambiguous space without the referenced interface.

en.question: On an OSPF ABR you configure 'area 2 filter-list prefix BLOCK in'. Which routes does this actually filter?
options: Type-1 and Type-2 LSAs inside Area 2, so internal routers of that area lose the denied prefixes from their own LSDB and SPF tree while the ABR keeps them in its routing table
Type-5 external LSAs from any ASBR, so redistributed routes matching the list are removed from every area, including the backbone, without touching inter-area summaries
Only the ABR's own routing table: the LSAs are still flooded into Area 2, but the ABR stops installing the denied prefixes and no longer forwards traffic toward them
Type-3 summary LSAs the ABR would originate into Area 2, so prefixes denied by the list are not advertised into that area as inter-area routes; intra-area LSAs are unaffected
en.explanation: 'area X filter-list prefix NAME in|out' is applied on an ABR and filters Type-3 summary LSAs: 'in' controls what is advertised into area X, 'out' what is advertised out of it. It does not filter Type-1/2 LSAs inside an area or Type-5 externals, and it changes what is flooded, not just the ABR's own routing table (that would be a distribute-list in).

en.question: R1 has Loopback0 10.50.0.1/24 in OSPF, but neighbors learn 10.50.0.1/32 instead of 10.50.0.0/24. Why, and how do you make OSPF advertise the /24?
options: OSPF treats a loopback as a stub host and advertises it as /32; setting 'ip ospf network point-to-point' on Loopback0 makes it advertise the configured /24 mask
The neighbors run auto-summary, which shortens every loopback to a host route; 'no auto-summary' under the OSPF process on each neighbor restores the /24 prefix
The loopback is in a stub area, which only allows host routes; converting the area to a normal area or a totally stubby area will advertise the configured /24 mask
OSPF hello packets carry only the router ID, so loopbacks always appear as /32; adding 'network 10.50.0.0 0.0.0.255 area 0' a second time forces a /24 Type-3 LSA
en.explanation: By default OSPF uses the LOOPBACK network type for loopback interfaces and advertises them as /32 host routes, whatever mask is configured. 'ip ospf network point-to-point' on the loopback makes OSPF advertise the real prefix (/24). OSPF has no auto-summary, stub areas do not restrict masks, and repeating the network statement changes nothing.

en.question: You enable 'neighbor 203.0.113.2 ttl-security hops 1' on an eBGP session to a directly connected ISP router. What does this mainly protect against?
options: It forces the ISP peer to send only communities you recognise, dropping any update whose COMMUNITY attribute is missing or marked no-export before the path is even considered for the Loc-RIB
It encrypts the TCP payload of BGP with IPsec using a PSK derived from the TTL value, so a packet with the wrong hop count fails integrity checks immediately and is discarded by the stack
It raises the BGP hold timer to match the IP TTL of each peer, so a speaker that is more than one Layer-3 hop away times out before it can inject a forged OPEN or UPDATE into the session
It accepts only BGP packets whose IP TTL proves they crossed at most one hop (typically arriving as TTL 255), blocking remote spoofed TCP sessions aimed at port 179
en.explanation: BGP TTL Security (GTSH) checks the IP TTL of incoming BGP packets. With hops 1 on a directly connected eBGP peer, the packet must arrive with TTL 255 (sent with 255 and decremented zero times across L3 hops), which remote attackers spoofing TCP/179 cannot easily forge from several hops away. It does not encrypt BGP, alter hold timers, or filter communities.

en.question: An ASBR originates a Type-5 LSA for 198.51.100.0/24 with a non-zero forwarding address of 10.9.9.1. Routers in the domain list the LSA but do not install the external route. What is the most likely cause?
options: A non-zero forwarding address is only legal in Type-7 LSAs, so every router discards the Type-5 as malformed and waits for the ASBR to resend it with 0.0.0.0
The external route is E2, and E2 routes are installed only when the ASBR is in the backbone area, so moving it to area 0 is the only fix for this behaviour
No OSPF intra-area or inter-area route to 10.9.9.1 exists, so routers cannot resolve the forwarding address and will not use that external LSA
The forwarding address must equal the ASBR router ID; when they differ, SPF treats the LSA as coming from a second ASBR and suppresses it as a duplicate
en.explanation: When a Type-5 LSA carries a non-zero forwarding address, routers must reach that address through an OSPF intra-area or inter-area route; if they cannot, the external route is not installed. A common cause is the FA subnet not being advertised into OSPF (for example a passive or missing network statement) or being filtered. Forwarding addresses are valid in Type-5 LSAs, E2 routes do not need the ASBR in area 0, and the FA does not have to match the router ID.

en.question: Area 2 is connected to the backbone only through area 1. You configure 'area 1 virtual-link 2.2.2.2' on both ABRs, but the virtual link never comes up. Area 1 is configured as 'area 1 stub'. What is the problem?
options: Virtual links need the two ABRs to be directly connected on the same subnet in area 1, so a multi-hop path through area 1 always keeps the link down
The virtual link must be configured under area 0 instead of area 1, because it belongs to the backbone and IOS ignores it when it names a normal area
Virtual links only work when area 2 is a totally stubby area, so area 2 must be changed before the ABRs can build a virtual adjacency through area 1
A virtual link cannot cross a stub area; the transit area must be a normal area, so area 1 has to stop being stub
en.explanation: An OSPF virtual link is a logical part of area 0 tunnelled through a transit area, and the transit area must carry full routing information. Stub, totally stubby and NSSA areas cannot be transit areas, so IOS will not bring the virtual link up while area 1 is stub. The ABRs do not need to share a subnet (the link follows the intra-area path to the other router ID), the command is entered with the transit area number, and area 2's type does not matter.

en.question: A router has eBGP sessions to ISP-A (AS 65001) and ISP-B (AS 65002). Both advertise 203.0.113.0/24 with equal attributes and an AS path of length 1. 'maximum-paths 2' is set, yet only one path is installed. Why?
options: By default eBGP multipath requires identical AS_PATH attributes; 'bgp bestpath as-path multipath-relax' allows different paths of equal length
The maximum-paths command only applies to iBGP routes, so eBGP routes from two providers need 'maximum-paths ibgp 2' before both are installed
BGP never installs more than one path for a prefix learned from different neighbour ASes, so load sharing needs a static route to each provider
Both paths must also have the same BGP router ID, so one provider has to change its router ID before the router treats them as equal-cost paths
en.explanation: For BGP multipath, candidate paths must match on weight, local preference, origin, MED and AS_PATH. Without extra configuration IOS demands the AS_PATH be identical, not just equally long, so paths via AS 65001 and AS 65002 are not multipath candidates. 'bgp bestpath as-path multipath-relax' loosens this to equal length. 'maximum-paths ibgp' is the iBGP knob, BGP can load share across ASes once relaxed, and the router ID is only a tie-breaker.

en.question: A branch router runs 'eigrp stub receive-only' towards the hub. The branch LAN 10.50.0.0/24 is in the EIGRP network statement and the adjacency is up, but the hub has no route to 10.50.0.0/24. Why?
options: The stub option stops the hub from forming a full adjacency, so it keeps the neighbour but ignores every update until the hold timer expires
Stub routers only send routes after the hub queries them, and the hub never queries a stub, so the LAN route appears only after a flap
receive-only makes the branch send its connected routes only as summaries, and the hub drops the summary because auto-summary is off
receive-only tells the branch to advertise no routes at all, so the hub learns nothing from it; use 'eigrp stub connected' to send the LAN
en.explanation: An EIGRP stub tells its neighbours not to query it, and the stub keyword decides what it advertises: connected, summary, static, redistributed, leak-map or receive-only. receive-only advertises nothing, so the hub learns no prefixes from the branch, even though the adjacency and the network statement are fine. The usual fix is 'eigrp stub connected summary' (the default) or at least 'connected', or a static route on the hub.

en.question: Two sites are joined by a GRE tunnel over the internet. Pings and SSH across the tunnel work, but HTTPS pages and file copies hang after the first few packets. The physical links have an MTU of 1500. What is the usual fix on the tunnel interfaces?
options: Set 'ip mtu 1400' and 'ip tcp adjust-mss 1360', so large TCP segments fit with the GRE and IP headers added
Set 'tunnel mode ipip', because GRE cannot carry TCP sessions longer than a few packets and IP-in-IP removes that limit
Set 'keepalive 10 3', because the tunnel goes down between keepalives and the long transfers are cut each time it does
Set 'bandwidth 1500' on the tunnel, because the default tunnel bandwidth is too low and large flows get policed to zero
en.explanation: GRE adds 24 bytes of headers, so a full 1500-byte packet no longer fits on a 1500-byte path. Small packets like pings and SSH keystrokes pass, but large TCP segments with DF set are dropped, and if ICMP 'fragmentation needed' is filtered, path MTU discovery fails and the session hangs. Lowering the tunnel IP MTU to 1400 and clamping the TCP MSS to 1360 avoids it. IP-in-IP has the same overhead problem, keepalives only track tunnel state and the bandwidth command only affects routing metrics and QoS.

en.question: An edge router has 'network 10.20.0.0 mask 255.255.0.0' under BGP. Its routing table holds 10.20.1.0/24, 10.20.2.0/24 and 10.20.3.0/24 learned through OSPF, but the ISP never receives 10.20.0.0/16. What is wrong?
options: The BGP network command only advertises classful networks, so a /16 inside 10.0.0.0/8 has to be written as 10.0.0.0
BGP never advertises prefixes learned through OSPF unless 'redistribute ospf' is also configured under the BGP process
The ISP filters every prefix longer than /8, so the /16 is dropped on arrival and the local router shows it as sent
The network command needs an exact match in the routing table; add 'ip route 10.20.0.0 255.255.0.0 Null0'
en.explanation: A BGP network statement is injected only when the routing table has that exact prefix and mask. The /24s don't match a /16, so nothing is sent. A static route to Null0 for 10.20.0.0/16 creates the exact entry (and drops traffic for unused parts of the range), or 'aggregate-address' can build the summary from the /24s. The mask keyword allows classless prefixes, OSPF routes can be advertised by a network statement when they match exactly, and the ISP never saw the prefix at all.

en.question: To lower the local preference of one prefix from an ISP, an engineer applies an inbound route-map with a single clause: 'route-map ISP-IN permit 10', 'match ip address prefix-list ONE', 'set local-preference 50'. After a soft reset, only that prefix is left from the ISP. Why?
options: A route-map ends with an implicit deny, so every prefix that doesn't match clause 10 is dropped; add an empty 'permit 20'
Setting local preference on one prefix makes BGP remove the others from the same neighbor, so the best path stays stable
The soft reset clears the whole BGP table, and the other prefixes will only come back after the next keepalive is received
Local preference 50 is below the default for that neighbor, so BGP marks the whole session as less preferred and filters it
en.explanation: Like an ACL, a route-map denies anything that matches no clause. Applied inbound, it keeps only the prefixes in list ONE and drops the rest. A final 'route-map ISP-IN permit 20' with no match statement lets all other routes through unchanged. Local preference is set per path and never removes other prefixes, a soft reset doesn't wait for a keepalive, and the session itself is not filtered.

pt.question: Na tríade CIA da segurança da informação, o que representa a Confidentiality (Confidencialidade)?
options: Garantir que os sistemas estão sempre disponíveis para utilizadores autorizados, mesmo em falha de hardware
Garantir que só entidades autorizadas acedem à informação, tipicamente com controlos de acesso e encriptação
Garantir que os dados não são alterados sem deteção, por exemplo com hashes criptográficos e assinaturas
Garantir que o tráfego de rede usa sempre a porta TCP 443, mesmo em redes internas isoladas da Internet
pt.explanation: A tríade CIA é Confidentiality, Integrity e Availability. Confidencialidade protege o acesso à informação (quem pode ver); Integridade protege contra alterações não autorizadas; Disponibilidade assegura acesso quando necessário.

pt.question: Um email pede-lhe urgentemente para clicar num link e «validar a conta Cisco» introduzindo a password. Que tipo de ataque de engenharia social é este?
options: Phishing (ou spear phishing se for direcionado)
Ataque de força bruta contra o servidor RADIUS
Man-in-the-middle exclusivamente na camada física
DDoS por amplificação DNS
pt.explanation: Phishing usa mensagens fraudulentas para induzir a vítima a revelar credenciais ou instalar malware. Spear phishing é a variante altamente personalizada. Não é força bruta, MITM físico nem DDoS.

pt.question: Qual é a diferença principal entre um firewall de filtragem de pacotes e um sistema IDS/IPS?
options: Um firewall só analisa malware em anexos de email SMTP; o IDS/IPS limita-se a fazer NAT entre endereços privados e públicos
O firewall e o IDS executam exatamente a mesma função; o IPS é apenas a marca comercial da Cisco para esse tipo de equipamento
O firewall aplica política de permitir/negar tráfego; o IDS deteta anomalias/assinaturas (alerta) e o IPS pode bloquear em linha
O IDS substitui completamente o AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) no controlo de identidade dos utilizadores
pt.explanation: Firewalls controlam o que passa segundo regras. IDS (Intrusion Detection) monitoriza e alerta; IPS (Intrusion Prevention) atua em linha e pode descartar tráfego malicioso. São complementares, não substitutos de AAA.

pt.question: No modelo AAA usado em redes Cisco, o que significam Authentication, Authorization e Accounting?
options: Apenas a encriptação de ligações VPN site-to-site com IPsec, sem identificar quem é o utilizador
Apenas o balanceamento de carga entre controladores wireless, sem autorizar o que cada sessão pode fazer
Apenas o inventário automático de switches na LAN, sem registar que utilizador acedeu nem o que fez
Autenticar quem é o utilizador/dispositivo, autorizar o que pode fazer, e registar (accounting) o que fez
pt.explanation: AAA: Authentication verifica identidade; Authorization define permissões/políticas; Accounting regista sessões e uso (útil para auditoria e faturação). Protocolos comuns: RADIUS e TACACS+.

pt.question: Em VPNs, qual afirmação descreve melhor IPsec em comparação com SSL/TLS VPN (ex.: acesso remoto via browser ou AnyConnect em modo SSL)?
options: IPsec opera tipicamente nas camadas de rede (protege pacotes IP) e é comum em site-to-site; SSL VPN trabalha sobretudo na sessão/transporte e é popular para acesso remoto de utilizadores
IPsec só funciona em IPv6 e recusa pacotes IPv4 no router; a SSL VPN só funciona em IPv4 e não estabelece qualquer sessão de acesso remoto quando o cliente usa apenas IPv6
A SSL VPN substitui sempre o routing OSPF no núcleo da rede, retirando as adjacências OSPF e passando a encaminhar todo o tráfego interno do campus apenas por túneis TLS
IPsec e a SSL VPN são exatamente o mesmo protocolo com nomes diferentes, com os mesmos cabeçalhos ESP, a mesma porta de transporte e a mesma negociação IKE de chaves
pt.explanation: IPsec (AH/ESP, IKE) protege tráfego IP e é clássico em VPNs site-to-site. SSL/TLS VPNs encapsulam sessões de utilizador e são comuns em remote access. Ambos podem coexistir conforme o caso de uso.

pt.question: Qual descrição corresponde corretamente a ransomware?
options: Malware que cifra ficheiros da vítima e exige pagamento (resgate) para devolver o acesso
Um protocolo proprietário da Cisco usado apenas para sincronizar relógios NTP internos
Uma ACL estendida que permite apenas tráfego HTTPS e bloqueia todo o restante da rede
Um tipo de cabo de fibra óptica multimodo usado em ligações curtas dentro do edifício
pt.explanation: Ransomware encripta dados e pede resgate. Outros tipos: vírus, worms, trojans, spyware, rootkits. Mitigações: backups offline, patching, MFA, filtragem de email e least privilege.

pt.question: O que é Zero Trust, em termos de princípios de segurança de rede?
options: Confiar automaticamente em qualquer dispositivo que esteja dentro da LAN corporativa, sem nova verificação de identidade
Desligar todos os firewalls de perímetro porque a cloud do fornecedor já é tratada como segura por predefinição, sem inspeção
Nunca confiar por predefinição: verificar continuamente identidade, contexto e postura antes de conceder acesso mínimo necessário
Usar apenas passwords partilhadas nos switches de acesso da LAN, sem autenticação individual de cada utilizador ou porta
pt.explanation: Zero Trust assume que a rede interna não é zona de confiança automática. Exige autenticação forte, autorização contextual, microsegmentação e verificação contínua (nunca trust, always verify).

pt.question: No ecossistema Cisco de segurança, qual o papel típico do Cisco ISE (Identity Services Engine) face a uma plataforma de XDR/visão unificada como SecureX (ou sucessoras)?
options: O ISE substitui completamente o routing BGP na Internet, anunciando os prefixos públicos e as rotas externas no lugar dos routers de fronteira da própria organização
O ISE foca-se em identidade, controlo de acesso (802.1X, guest, posture) e policy; plataformas tipo SecureX agregam telemetria e orquestram resposta entre produtos
O SecureX é apenas um cabo de consola série ligado à porta de consola do router; o ISE é só um tema de wallpaper decorativo no ecrã inicial do equipamento
Ambos servem exclusivamente para configurar VLANs de acesso em switches não geridos, sem qualquer função de identidade, de posture ou de orquestração
pt.explanation: Cisco ISE é o cérebro de AAA/policy NAC (802.1X, profiling, posture, guest). SecureX (e evoluções) integra alertas e workflows entre firewall, endpoint, email, etc. São complementares na arquitetura de segurança Cisco.

pt.question: Qual é a diferença fundamental entre hashing e encriptação simétrica?
options: Hashing e encriptação são sempre o mesmo algoritmo AES-256, com a mesma chave secreta e o mesmo resultado reversível nos dois casos
A encriptação só funciona em texto escrito em português; o hashing só produz um resultado válido quando o texto original está em inglês
O hashing aumenta sempre o tamanho dos dados de origem em cada bloco; a encriptação simétrica reduz sempre a mensagem para exatamente 128 bits
Hashing é tipicamente unidirecional (integridade/verificação); encriptação simétrica é reversível com a chave partilhada (confidencialidade)
pt.explanation: Hashes (SHA-256, etc.) não se «desfazem» para recuperar o original — servem para integridade e verificação. Encriptação simétrica (AES) cifra e decifra com a mesma chave. Assimétrico usa pares de chaves pública/privada.

pt.question: Porque é que a autenticação multifator (MFA) reduz significativamente o risco de compromisso de contas?
options: Porque elimina por completo a necessidade de patches de segurança no sistema operativo, deixando as falhas do software sem correção
Porque torna o Wi-Fi automaticamente WPA3 sem qualquer configuração, mesmo em pontos de acesso antigos que só suportam WPA2
Porque substitui os firewalls perimetrais em todos os cenários, dispensando as regras de filtragem na fronteira da rede
Porque exige algo mais do que só a password (ex.: app OTP, token, biometria), dificultando o uso de credenciais roubadas
pt.explanation: MFA combina fatores (conhecimento, posse, inerência). Mesmo com password vazada, o atacante precisa do segundo fator. É controlo essencial em Zero Trust e em acesso administrativo Cisco (e não substitui patching nem firewalls).

pt.question: O que é defense in depth (defesa em profundidade) num ambiente de rede?
options: Usar uma única password complexa para todos os dispositivos, partilhada entre os routers, os switches e os firewalls da rede local
Confiar apenas num antivirus no endpoint e remover a segmentação, deixando a LAN interna como uma única zona de confiança
Aplicar várias camadas de controlos (perímetro, rede, identidade, endpoint, dados) para que a falha de um não comprometa tudo
Desativar os logs de segurança para melhorar a performance do equipamento, sem registar tentativas de acesso nem alterações
pt.explanation: Defense in depth sobrepõe controlos complementares: firewalls, segmentação, AAA/MFA, EDR, encriptação, monitorização. Reduz o impacto de uma única falha.

pt.question: Qual o benefício principal da segmentação de rede (ex.: VLANs, firewalls entre zonas) para a cibersegurança?
options: Aumentar o broadcast domain de cada VLAN para que o malware se propague mais depressa entre hosts da mesma zona e das zonas vizinhas
Eliminar a necessidade de atualizar o firmware dos switches, firewalls e routers, tratando a segmentação como substituto dos patches
Permitir que convidados usem a mesma VLAN de gestão dos routers e firewalls, com acesso direto aos endereços IP de administração
Limitar movimento lateral: um compromisso numa zona não tem acesso automático a servidores críticos noutra zona
pt.explanation: Segmentação (e microsegmentação) restringe east-west traffic. Isola IoT/guest da gestão e de data centers, alinhado com Zero Trust e least privilege.

pt.question: Qual é o objetivo principal de uma plataforma SIEM (Security Information and Event Management)?
options: Substituir todos os agentes antivírus de endpoint por um único packet broker no switch core, que passa a analisar os ficheiros maliciosos no host
Emitir certificados TLS públicos para servidores internos sem uma CA privada, assinando os nomes internos como se fosse uma autoridade pública
Recolher e correlacionar logs/eventos de muitas fontes, detetar padrões suspeitos e apoiar alertas e investigação
Garantir zero falsos positivos bloqueando todas as consultas DNS de saída, para que nenhum nome externo seja resolvido pelos clientes
pt.explanation: Um SIEM agrega logs e eventos de segurança (firewalls, endpoints, identidade, cloud, etc.), normaliza e correlaciona-os, e ajuda analistas a detetar, alertar e investigar incidentes. Não substitui AV por um packet broker, não funciona como CA pública de TLS, e não promete zero falsos positivos ao bloquear DNS às cegas.

pt.question: Em cibersegurança, para que se usa principalmente o framework MITRE ATT&CK?
options: Um guia de sintaxe CLI específico de fabricante para configurar access lists no ASA, com os comandos access-list e access-group, a ordem das ACEs e o implicit deny no fim de cada ACL
Uma base de conhecimento de táticas e técnicas de adversários (e procedimentos relacionados) usada para mapear deteções, planear defesas e falar de ameaças numa linguagem comum
Um algoritmo de encriptação obrigatório que substitui o AES em todos os handshakes TLS 1.3, forçando uma única cifra simétrica em cada ClientHello e recusando as outras suites negociadas
Uma norma de layout físico de racks para densidade de cablagem em data centers, que fixa a altura em U, as calhas verticais e o espaçamento dos patch panels de cobre e de fibra
pt.explanation: O MITRE ATT&CK cataloga táticas (o «porquê») e técnicas (o «como») de adversários no mundo real, muitas vezes com exemplos de procedimentos. Os defensores usam-no para analisar falhas de cobertura, escrever deteções e discutir incidentes de forma consistente. Não é documentação CLI do ASA, não é uma cifra que substitui o AES, e não é uma norma de cablagem.

pt.question: Contra o que é que um Web Application Firewall (WAF) protege principalmente?
options: Ataques à camada de aplicação contra apps HTTP/HTTPS (por exemplo SQLi, XSS e abuso de URLs ou APIs vulneráveis), inspecionando e filtrando pedidos web
Cortes de cabo Layer 1 entre o switch de acesso e o PC do utilizador, quando o par de cobre ou a fibra perde continuidade e o link Ethernet fica sem sinal na tomada
Esgotamento de memória da LSDB OSPF nos routers core causado por demasiados LSAs Type 5 de rotas externas redistribuídas a partir de outros protocolos
Falha da bateria de um UPS que alimenta os wireless controllers, deixando os access points sem energia durante um corte elétrico no bastidor
pt.explanation: Um WAF fica à frente de aplicações web e inspeciona tráfego HTTP/S para bloquear ou desafiar ataques comuns à camada de aplicação, como SQL injection, cross-site scripting e padrões de pedido conhecidos como maus. Não resolve cortes físicos de cabo, dimensionamento da LSDB OSPF, nem baterias de UPS.

pt.question: Qual é o objetivo principal do DNSSEC?
options: Encriptar cada consulta DNS para que o resolver recursivo nunca veja o nome pedido (isso é DNS over TLS ou DNS over HTTPS, não DNSSEC) e o QNAME fique oculto no trajeto de rede
Substituir o SPF para que os servidores de correio deixem de verificar que hosts podem enviar pelo domínio, ignorando o registo TXT e aceitando qualquer MTA
Assinar digitalmente os dados DNS para que os resolvers validadores detetem respostas forjadas ou alteradas (autenticidade e integridade), sem esconder a própria consulta
Bloquear automaticamente todas as transferências de malware no endpoint, apagando o ficheiro descarregado antes de qualquer processo o conseguir executar
pt.explanation: O DNSSEC acrescenta assinaturas digitais (registos RRSIG e DNSKEY, encadeados com DS no pai) para um resolver validador confirmar que os dados vieram da zona autoritativa e não foram modificados. A confidencialidade da consulta vem de DoT ou DoH, não do DNSSEC. Não substitui a autenticação de email nem a proteção de endpoint.

pt.question: Em conjunto, o que fazem SPF, DKIM e DMARC na segurança do correio eletrónico?
options: Encriptam o corpo da mensagem de ponta a ponta para só o destinatário a poder ler (isso é S/MIME ou PGP), cifrando o conteúdo com a chave pública do destinatário antes da submissão de correio ao MTA
O SPF indica que servidores podem enviar em nome do domínio, o DKIM assina criptograficamente a mensagem e o DMARC diz aos recetores o que fazer quando essas verificações falham e como reportar
Analisam anexos à procura de ransomware dentro do MTA, abrindo cada parte MIME e bloqueando a entrega quando a assinatura do payload coincide com malware conhecido
Substituem o TLS na submissão SMTP (porta 587), dispensando o STARTTLS e o certificado porque a política publicada do domínio autentica sozinha o canal com o relay
pt.explanation: O SPF autoriza hosts de envio num registo TXT de DNS. O DKIM assina cabeçalhos selecionados e o corpo com uma chave do domínio publicada em DNS. O DMARC exige que o domínio visível do From alinhe com SPF e/ou DKIM e publica uma política (none, quarantine ou reject) mais relatórios. Em conjunto combatem a falsificação do domínio; não encriptam a mensagem nem substituem o TLS do SMTP.

pt.question: Qual é a diferença principal entre EDR e XDR?
options: O EDR só encripta discos com uma chave de volume no endpoint; o XDR só configura VLANs de acesso nos switches, sem recolher telemetria de processos, ficheiros ou comportamento do host nem cruzar alertas de outras ferramentas de segurança
