options: A cryptographic file hash (e.g. SHA-256)
The colour of the desktop background
The printer model in most production environments
The office zip code
en.explanation: File hashes uniquely fingerprint samples so the same malware can be recognized across hosts and threat intel feeds.

en.question: Why do SOC analysts learn basic regular expressions?
options: To match and extract patterns in logs and packet data efficiently
To replace the need for firewalls when no other controls exist
To assign IP addresses in most production environments
To configure RAID in most production environments according to common practice
en.explanation: Regex lets analysts quickly filter and extract patterns (IPs, URLs, hashes) from large log and PCAP datasets.

en.question: What does vulnerability management mainly involve?
options: Identifying, prioritizing and remediating weaknesses over time
Only buying new firewalls during routine maintenance windows
Only resetting passwords monthly without additional tooling
Only painting server racks according to common practice when no other controls exist
en.explanation: Vulnerability management is the ongoing process of finding, ranking and fixing weaknesses across the estate.

en.question: According to NIST SP 800-61, which activity belongs to the Preparation phase?
options: Building playbooks, contacts and tooling before an incident
Deleting all evidence after an incident
Ignoring alerts in most production environments
Sharing passwords on a whiteboard for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: Preparation covers policies, playbooks, contacts, tooling and training so the team can respond effectively when an incident occurs.

en.question: According to the order of volatility, which evidence should be captured before a disk image?
options: CPU registers and RAM contents
Archived tape backups from last year
Printed manuals
Wall posters when no other controls exist
en.explanation: Volatile data (CPU, RAM, network state) disappears on power-off, so it is collected before less volatile storage such as disk images.

en.question: Which element is used when profiling a network for anomaly detection?
options: Typical throughput, session duration, ports and critical asset address space
The colour of the patch cables in typical enterprise networks
The brand of the chairs for day-to-day operations in most production environments
The font used in emails in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: Network profiling baselines throughput, session lengths, ports in use and critical ranges so deviations stand out.

en.question: When profiling a server for security, which item is useful to baseline?
options: Listening ports, logged-in users, running processes and applications
The wallpaper image during routine maintenance windows
The keyboard language only when no other controls exist
The desk height according to common practice when no other controls exist
en.explanation: Server profiling notes listening ports, accounts, processes and apps so unexpected services or users become visible.

en.question: Which data type is protected health information (PHI)?
options: Medical records identifying a patient
A public weather forecast
An open-source software license
A network cable length in most production environments
en.explanation: PHI is health information that can identify an individual and is protected under frameworks such as HIPAA.

en.question: What do SOC metrics such as time-to-detect and time-to-contain measure?
options: How quickly the team finds and limits an incident
How fast printers print during routine maintenance windows
How bright the SOC lights are in typical enterprise networks
How many coffee cups are used
en.explanation: SOC metrics like TTD/TTC/TTR quantify response speed so the organisation can improve detection and containment.

en.question: In a suspicious DNS query seen in a PCAP, which fields are most useful to inspect?
options: Query name, query type and response addresses
Only the Ethernet FCS during routine maintenance windows
Only the IP TTL according to common practice
Only the TCP window size
en.explanation: DNS analysis focuses on the queried name, type (A/AAAA/TXT/MX) and the answers returned, which often reveal C2 or tunneling.

en.question: What does a buffer overflow endpoint attack mainly try to achieve?
options: Overwrite memory to alter program control flow
Improve memory safety during routine maintenance windows
Compress the binary in typical enterprise networks
Update the BIOS securely
en.explanation: A buffer overflow writes past a buffer's bounds to corrupt memory and often hijack control flow for arbitrary code execution.

en.question: What is threat hunting?
options: Proactively searching for threats that automated detections may have missed
Waiting for vendors to email indicators according to common practice
Deleting all logs weekly during routine maintenance windows
Disabling EDR to reduce noise when no other controls exist in most production environments
en.explanation: Threat hunting is a proactive, hypothesis-driven search for adversary activity that existing alerts may not have caught.

en.question: What does DevSecOps emphasize?
options: Integrating security into the CI/CD pipeline instead of treating it as a final gate
Removing all automated tests without additional tooling in typical enterprise networks
Shipping without any reviews in most production environments
Storing secrets in source code in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: DevSecOps builds security into development and delivery pipelines (scanning, policy as code) rather than bolting it on at the end.

en.question: An analyst sees a Windows Security log with many 4625 failures followed by a 4624 for the same account from an unusual IP. What does this pattern most suggest?
options: Possible brute-force that eventually succeeded
A successful disk defragmentation
A normal DHCP renew across mixed vendor fleets
A printer firmware update
en.explanation: Repeated logon failures (4625) then a success (4624) from an odd source is a classic sign of a successful brute-force or spraying attack.

en.question: What characterizes a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack?
options: Many coordinated sources overwhelm a target's capacity
A single user mistypes a password once
A scheduled antivirus scan
A firmware update window in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: DDoS uses many (often botnet) sources to flood a target beyond its capacity, making service unavailable.

en.question: What kind of data does Application Visibility and Control (AVC) typically add?
options: Identification of applications beyond just port numbers
Only Layer-1 signal strength when no other controls exist
Only the serial numbers of switches
Only the office temperature in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: AVC classifies traffic by application (not just port), enabling policies and monitoring based on what apps are actually in use.

en.question: An alert shows a proxy log for a rare domain, an IPS signature hit on the same flow, and NetFlow with a large outbound byte count. What should the analyst do first?
options: Correlate the sources to confirm a real exfiltration or C2 case
Ignore all three because they conflict for day-to-day operations
Delete the NetFlow in typical enterprise networks
Disable the proxy according to common practice
en.explanation: Multiple independent sensors agreeing on the same flow raises confidence; correlate timestamps, IPs and users before containment.

en.question: Which cloud-specific threat involves stealing API keys that grant broad access to cloud resources?
options: Compromised credentials and insecure APIs
Cable cut at the ISP for day-to-day operations
Printer paper jam according to common practice
Monitor backlight failure
en.explanation: Cloud breaches often stem from leaked API keys or weak APIs that grant wide access to storage and compute resources.

en.question: What is a prompt injection attack against an AI/LLM system?
options: Crafting input that overrides the model's instructions to make it leak data or act wrongly
Injecting SQL into a database via a form during routine maintenance windows
Flooding a VPN concentrator in most production environments in typical enterprise networks
Overwriting BIOS firmware for day-to-day operations in most production environments
en.explanation: Prompt injection crafts user input that hijacks or overrides the system prompt, causing data leakage or unintended actions.

en.question: What does 'system prompt leakage' risk in an LLM deployment?
options: Exposing hidden instructions that reveal policies or secrets to the user
Losing the GPU driver across mixed vendor fleets in most production environments
Breaking DHCP leases during routine maintenance windows
Disabling syslog for day-to-day operations without additional tooling
en.explanation: If an LLM reveals its hidden system prompt, attackers learn policies, tool instructions or secrets embedded there.

en.question: Why is post-quantum cryptography (PQC) becoming relevant for security architects?
options: Large quantum computers may break widely used public-key algorithms
PQC makes Wi-Fi faster across mixed vendor fleets during routine maintenance windows
PQC replaces Ethernet cables in most production environments
PQC removes the need for MFA without additional tooling
en.explanation: PQC algorithms are designed to resist attacks from large-scale quantum computers that could break RSA and ECC.

en.question: What is MASQUE in modern encrypted transport?
options: A set of HTTP/3 mechanisms to proxy traffic over QUIC
A Layer-2 spanning-tree variant
A Windows event ID according to common practice
A RADIUS attribute for VLANs without additional tooling
en.explanation: MASQUE (Multiplexed Application Substrate over QUIC Encryption) defines HTTP/3 proxying so traffic can be securely relayed over QUIC.

en.question: Which Cisco VPN technology builds hub-and-spoke or spoke-to-spoke IPsec overlays with NHRP?
options: DMVPN
GETVPN
SSL clientless portal only
L2TP without IPsec
